title: Dhurandhar 2's Uncensored 'Raw' Cut Is Already on Netflix. Unless You're in India. Then You Wait Until June 4 and Get the Sanitised Version.
excerpt: NRIs in the US, UK, and Canada have been watching the uncut version of the biggest Indian film of 2026 for days. Indian audiences still have to wait for the CBFC-approved cut on JioHotstar. The irony writes itself.
body:
Here is a fact that perfectly captures the absurdity of India's content regulation landscape in 2026: the biggest Indian film of the year, made in India, set in India, starring an Indian actor, about Indian intelligence operations — is available in its full, uncut form to audiences in 190 countries. Except India. Where it was made.

Dhurandhar 2: The Revenge, Ranveer Singh's spy thriller directed by Aditya Dhar, has been streaming globally on Netflix in its raw, uncensored version since late May. The cut includes graphic violence, expletives, and sequences that the CBFC trimmed or muted for the theatrical release. It is, by most accounts, the version Aditya Dhar intended audiences to see.

Indian audiences will get the film on JioHotstar on June 4. They will get the CBFC-approved theatrical cut. The uncut version is not currently planned for Indian streaming.

## The Numbers Are Already Historic

Before we get to the streaming politics, let us acknowledge what this film has accomplished in theatres. As of Day 68, Dhurandhar 2 has earned approximately ₹1,148 crore net in India — making it comfortably the second highest-grossing Hindi film in domestic box office history. Worldwide, the gross stands at approximately ₹1,800 crore. The opening week alone delivered ₹674 crore net.

The film is still running in theatres in its ninth week. Daily collections have dipped to ₹30 lakh, but it refuses to leave screens entirely. Extended runs used to be a specialty of 1990s multi-starrer epics. Dhurandhar 2 is doing it in an era when most films vanish after two weekends.

## The Two Versions of the Same Film

Netflix's global release is being marketed as the "Raw" or "Undekha" (unseen) version. Reports indicate it includes sequences excised by the CBFC for the Indian theatrical release — including more explicit depictions of the intelligence operations at the film's core and unbleeped dialogue. The distinction matters because Aditya Dhar has spoken publicly about how the CBFC cuts altered the rhythm of certain scenes.

JioHotstar, which holds the Indian streaming rights, confirmed a June 4 premiere date. The version will be the theatrical cut — the same one that has earned ₹1,148 crore. There is no official confirmation of whether the raw cut will eventually be available in India on any platform.

## What This Means for NRIs

For the diaspora, this is both familiar and newly frustrating. NRIs have long dealt with geographic streaming restrictions — a Hindi film available on JioHotstar in India but not abroad, a Hollywood film on Netflix US but not Netflix India. What makes Dhurandhar 2 different is the content asymmetry.

An NRI in Houston can watch the uncut version on Netflix right now. The version the filmmaker intended. Their cousin in Hyderabad cannot. The cousin will get the same film, minus the parts the government decided they should not see, eight days later.

This is not a piracy issue. Both versions are legitimate, licensed releases. It is a regulatory issue — the CBFC's writ does not extend to Netflix's global catalogue, only to content specifically released in India. So the same film exists simultaneously in two official forms, and your geographic location determines which one you are allowed to watch.

## The Larger Pattern

Dhurandhar 2 is not the first film to have a different cut available internationally. But it is the highest-profile example of a growing trend: Indian filmmakers creating "director's cut" or "raw" versions for international platforms while accepting censorship for the domestic market. The incentive structure is clear — the theatrical box office in India is too valuable to antagonise the CBFC, but the global streaming audience is now large enough to justify a separate release.

For Netflix, the raw cut is a subscriber acquisition play. Indian diaspora audiences are a massive and growing segment of their international user base. Offering them the version they cannot get at home is a strategic move that costs Netflix nothing (the content is already produced) and earns them goodwill in a fiercely competitive streaming market.

For Indian audiences, it raises uncomfortable questions about who gets to see art as the artist intended it. The CBFC has long argued that its mandate is to protect Indian audiences from content deemed unsuitable. But in 2026, when any Indian with a VPN can access the Netflix global catalogue, the argument is more performative than practical.

## The Streaming War Continues

JioHotstar's June 4 date is strategically timed. The theatrical run will be in its tenth week by then, and daily collections will have fallen below ₹20 lakh. The OTT premiere will likely generate a massive spike in subscriptions — Dhurandhar 2 is the kind of event that sells platforms.

Whether Indian streaming eventually gets the raw cut remains an open question. For now, the geography of what you can watch remains one of the quieter absurdities of being Indian in 2026.
